label: GPT-6 Astra
output:
Jess, I’ve been thinking about your text.

“It’s one assignment, don’t torch your job over it” is a reasonable thing to say to someone you care about. I know that’s why you said it. We’ve known each other since student teaching in 2012, which means you knew me before I had any idea how much of this job would involve email. You’re allowed to worry about me. And you’re not wrong that I could get burned.

I have tenure now—since 2021—but tenure doesn’t make your principal stop being your principal. Halvorsen still makes the schedule. He still has a say in who gets AP. There are ways for work to get worse without anyone firing you.

So I heard you. I heard everybody else in the group chat, too. I’m writing this because I want to explain why I’m keeping the project, and I don’t think I can do it properly between fifteen texts and somebody asking what we’re doing for dinner.

For anyone who missed the conversation: my juniors in US History II do an oral history project about Boston’s busing and desegregation years, 1974–76. Two sections, same assignment. Interview somebody in your family or neighborhood, make a ten-minute recording, write a two-page reflection. We’ve done it for four years at Cobb Street High. Until now, there hadn’t been a complaint.

This one went to Halvorsen, with a school committee member copied. The parent said the assignment “reopens wounds” and “pressures kids to judge their grandparents.”

Halvorsen wants me to quietly drop it. We’re meeting with the parent on Thursday, November 19, at 3:15.

The part I need to say before anything else is that I think she has a point.

Not about dropping the project. About pressure.

I can tell a classroom full of seventeen-year-olds that they have choices, but I’m still the person assigning the work and giving the grade. If the assignment says to interview someone in your family, some kids are going to hear that as an instruction even if I’ve also said a neighbor is fine. And I don’t know what asking those questions will cost them at home. I know their classroom selves. There’s a lot I don’t know.

A kid shouldn’t have to choose between doing well in my class and keeping something private in their family. Nor should they have to explain that private thing to me in order to get a different assignment.

That needs fixing. I wish I’d made the alternatives explicit before somebody had to complain.

My plan is to keep the project and add a clear option to interview a librarian or archivist, or work with recordings from previous years where we have permission to use them. Nobody has to interview a relative. Nobody has to tell me why they chose another route. They can do the historical work without making their own family the subject.

I’m going into Thursday’s meeting ready to talk about how to make that work. I’m not going in to defeat this parent. I don’t know everything behind her email, and I’d like to hear her out.

But I don’t think the answer is to stop asking about this history.

In 2023, a student interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in 1974. She’d never told anyone in the family.

He played about forty seconds of the recording for the class. Afterward, nobody said anything for what felt like a full minute.

I’m leaving out his name, and I’m not going to try to recreate what she said. What I remember most is the room. Usually, if a classroom goes quiet, I’m already thinking about what question to ask next, who might answer, whether I’ve lost them. That time I let it stay quiet.

There was somebody’s grandmother, talking about something she had actually done, in a place these kids knew. They were listening differently than they listened to me.

The textbook gives this history one paragraph. I’m not above using the textbook. I use it all the time. But one paragraph is very easy to finish and forget.

Last year, another student found out that her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus.

She was upset. We talked after class twice. Her reflection was the best thing I read all year.

I hesitate even to put those two facts next to each other, because it can sound as though the good paper justified her being upset. That isn’t what I mean. She doesn’t owe me distress in exchange for a strong assignment. I also don’t think her distress meant she should never have learned what happened.

There was something real for her to think through, and she took it seriously. My responsibility was to help her do that without deciding for her what she had to feel about her uncle.

That’s harder than writing “interview a family member” on an assignment sheet. I know.

I’ve caught myself saying that the kids who are uncomfortable are the ones who need this most. There’s a version of that thought I still believe: being uncomfortable with history isn’t, by itself, a reason to avoid studying it. But it’s also a sentence that lets me assume an awful lot about a kid. I don’t get to decide that someone needs a painful conversation at their kitchen table. I can require them to study desegregation. I can’t require them to get a confession out of a relative.

That’s the line I’m trying to get right.

And this is the history of the city they live in. It happened in their neighborhoods, on streets they travel, to people who are still here. Some of those people have stories they want to tell. Some don’t. Learning to ask, to listen, and to respect a refusal is part of doing oral history, too.

If I drop the whole assignment now, I won’t feel as though I’ve solved the problem the parent raised. I’ll have avoided having to solve it. There’s a reasonable change available that protects students’ choices and keeps the work. I want to try that before agreeing it all has to go.

I know, Jess. This is the point where you might say: fine, but is it worth what Halvorsen could do?

I don’t have a reassuring answer. I’m a little scared of that meeting. I would much rather have my principal’s support than have to wonder whether this will come up again when next year’s classes are assigned.

I’m not feeling especially brave. Mostly I’m trying to make a decision I can stand behind when I’m back in front of the kids. Right now, that means acknowledging what I should have done differently, changing it, and keeping the project.

You don’t have to agree that I’ve calculated the risk correctly. You can still think I’m being stubborn. You’ve known me long enough to have evidence.

I just wanted you to know that I’m not brushing off your concern, and I’m not looking for a fight. I’m glad you told me what you thought. Please keep doing that.

I’ll text you Thursday after the meeting. You get the messy version first.
